newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - GI Elvis still a smash hit in Germany.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - GI Elvis still a smash hit in Germany.

text.p: For many, the 20th anniversary of Elvis Presley's death will bring to mind images of the King of Rock and Roll towards the end of his reign, washed up on a sea of junk food and drug dependency.
But the residents of the small German towns where he spent his U.S. military service cherish the memory of a very different Elvis -- a polite young star in his prime who felt at home here.

"He was such a handsome young man. He had a habit of bowing, which made an excellent impression on us," said Rita Issberner-Haldane, owner of the Hotel Grunewald in Bad Nauheim, where Elvis and his entourage lived for around four months.
Sadly, Elvis's bodyguards did not make such a good impression on the genteel clientele of the small hotel in this spa town, half an hour's drive north of Frankfurt.

Elvis and his companions -- his father, his secretary and his grandmother, who cooked pea soup for him on a small stove in the corner of her room -- all had to move out after the guards set fire to newspaper strips under his bedroom door for a prank.
Elvis did his 17-month military service at Ray Barracks in the neighbouring town of Friedberg, arriving in October 1958.

"We ran to the railway station and waited for him, full of joy and hoping maybe to get an autograph," recalled Ulrich Kiefer, a Friedberg councillor, who experienced Germany's Elvis mania as a 15-year-old schoolboy.

"It was a great experience for us, as young boys at that time," he said. "We were moulded by this rock music. It was a beautiful time for us. And then to see the person who embodied this music was a fantastic experience."
PAYING HOMAGE TO THE KING
Today Kiefer is at the centre of a drive to honour Elvis in the area where he spent a period which some experts believe was one of the happiest of his life.
Kiefer was behind a decision in 1995 to name a square in the town's main street "Elvis Presley Platz". The only other square named after Elvis is in Memphis, he proudly states.
But Presley pilgrims could be forgiven for being slightly underwhelmed.

Apart from the square, with a picture of Elvis in military uniform and a short biography, and an enterprising local woman who sells Elvis fruit tea, there is little trace of the king in this quiet town with a population of around 26,000.
There is no King of Rock and Roll record store, Graceland Garage or themed burger bar. Even asking for Elvis Presley Platz will get you blank looks at the local railway station.

Bad Nauheim has unveiled a small Elvis memorial outside the Hotel Grunewald -- a mixed blessing for the town council, which regularly has to send workers round to remove the lipstick of adoring fans who have kissed the king's white marble lips.
CELEBRATING A SPECIAL LEGACY
Town clerk Wolfgang Unkel is also keen to exploit Bad Nauheim's status as "Elvis's second home", saying the memorial has already given the local tourist industry a boost.
"Because here in Germany there is only this one point, this monument to Elvis, we know that people come every year who want to follow in Elvis's footsteps," he said.
"Elvis wrote musical history and the residents of this town are happy that he lived here and of course they're also proud."
The anniversary of Elvis's death on August 16 will be marked by a special festival in Friedberg, ending with a procession to the monument in Bad Nauheim, a few kilometres (miles) away.
A record company also plans to unveil a special "Bad Nauheim Medley" box set of Elvis CDs.
Unkel and Kiefer would like to see an annual Elvis festival and other ventures to promote their towns' rock roots.

Officials insist reports of a feud between the towns over which has the right to claim Elvis as its own were largely manufactured by the media when both the square and the memorial were unveiled two years ago.
But Bad Nauheimers point out that while Elvis worked in Friedberg, he chose to live in their town, renting a local villa for the rest of his tour of duty after he left the Grunewald.
NO GI BLUES IN GERMANY
There is little left to connect Elvis with Ray Barracks itself, except a small Elvis Room sandwiched between World War Two vehicles and Gulf War equipment in the barracks museum.
The small room contains pictures of Elvis in uniform and other memorabilia, such as a cover of his hit "Wooden Heart", based on a German folk song he heard during his time here.
The old chair where local barber Karl-Heinz Stein used to cut the king's hair is also in the room.
"I do believe this tour of duty in Friedberg and Bad Nauheim were some of the happiest hours in the life of the star," Stein writes in a note for visitors.
"His private affairs were orderly and straightened out. He did not rush from one appointment to the other and did not feel any urge to succeed at all costs."
Soldiers in accommodation block 3707, where the king spent his first few nights on German soil before moving to Bad Nauheim are respectful of the building's history but not awe-struck.
"It's just a barracks. He's a legacy but I don't really have any special feelings," said Sergeant First Class Kerry Heflin of Miami, Florida, serving with the 136 Infantry Batallion.
Back in the more luxurious surroundings of the Grunewald, the legacy is more tangible. The second floor which Elvis and his entourage rented has been left almost exactly as it was.

Selected fans can even stay in Room 10 -- Elvis's bedroom. The lean young star would stroll out onto the balcony there to greet his assembled fans below -- a world away from the bloated figure battling against drugs in later life.
"When you see what became of him, it makes you sad inside," laments Issberner-Haldane.
